description: The objective of the Rodent Research-9 (RR-9) mission was to use mice to understand the molecular basis of phenomena that affect astronauts during long-duration spaceflight, particularly visual impairment, and joint tissue degradation. To this end, a flight group (FLT) of 10-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were launched from Kennedy Space Center (KSC) on 8/14/2017 and housed in Rodent Habitats on the ISS for 33 days before being returned alive to Earth. After splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, the animals were transported to Loma Linda University (LLU) for testing, euthanasia, and dissection on 9/18/2018. Ground Control (GC) studies were planned to commence at KSC approximately one-week after the conclusion of the flight experiments. However, all the GC mouse studies at KSC had to be cancelled due to Hurricane Irma and potential adverse effects on the animal housing facility. The GC studies were therefore rescheduled and begun in May 2018. The GC was euthanized and dissected 6/18/2018 - 6/20/2018. Because this resulted in a different cohort of mice being used for the GC controls as compared to the flight (FLT) groups, two cohort controls were included in the study. The first, Cohort Control 1 (CC_C1), was from the same cohort as the FLT animals and was sacrificed and dissected 4 days after the FLT group (9/22/2017). The second, Cohort Control 2 (CC_C2), was from the same cohort as the GC, and was sacrificed and dissected 2-8 days after the GC, (6/24/2018 - 6/26/2018). The CC_C1 and CC_C2 groups were housed in standard cages and fed standard chow in contrast to all other groups which received Rodent Foodbars. Upon dissection, thymus tissues were preserved in liquid nitrogen and stored at 80 C before RNA was extracted. Only the flight (FLT, n of 10) and Ground Control (GC, n of 10) samples were processed and analyzed in this study. Libraries were generated using a 3’ Tag-seq approach and sequenced at a targeted depth of 40 M clusters (SE 93 bp).
funding: The sequencing analysis was funded by the NASA Space Biology program within the NASA Science Mission Directorate's (SMD) Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division.

payloads.description:
The Rodent Research 9 (RR-9) payload consisted of three space biology experiments that examined the impacts of long-duration spaceflight on human tissue and systems, aiming to better understand the visual impairment and joint tissue degradation that affected astronauts and to investigate possible ways to counteract those health problems. One investigation studied the effects of microgravity on fluid shifts and increased fluid pressures that occurred in the head. A second examined the impact of spaceflight on the vessels that supplied blood to the eyes. The third investigated the extent of knee and hip joint degradation caused by prolonged exposure to weightlessness.

NASA's Space Life and Physical Sciences (SLPS) partnered with Russia's Institute of Biomedical Problems (IMBP) to establish a collaborative and multidisciplinary study to examine the effects of spaceflight on various physiological systems. This mission was sponsored by the NASA Space Biology Program.

The objectives of the Investigator team’s studies were to evaluate physiological changes in mice that occurred during a long-duration spaceflight mission in low Earth orbit. Maximal science return was achieved by distributing dissected tissues from the animals to as many Russian and NASA investigators as possible via the SLPS Biospecimen Sharing Program (BSP) and through agreements with the IMBP.

Twenty (20) mice (male, C57BL/6) between 8–16 weeks old were launched in one Transporter (10 mice per side), transferred to Rodent Habitats onboard the International Space Station (ISS), and maintained in microgravity for approximately 30 days (the SpaceX Dragon docked period). Nominally, no crew activities were required except for standard animal transfers between the Transporter and Habitats, and other activities required to ensure animal welfare, such as health checks and NuRFB replenishments.

Prior to Dragon unberth, all twenty mice were transferred into a clean Transporter, followed by transfer to a Dragon capsule and then returned to Earth alive (live animal return [LAR]). The duration from splashdown to handover of the mice payload was approximately 48–72 hours. After the handover of the mice to the NASA Rodent Research team, the mice were immediately transported to a facility approved for conducting post-flight rodent gait assessment and dissections. This facility was located as close to the payload handover location as possible to minimize the total duration the mice were exposed to 1G post-splashdown. The primary investigator teams, BSP teams, and the Rodent Research dissection Lead and team conducted the dissection process at this facility immediately following a health check, specimen sampling, and acquisition of walking kinematic data.

The Rodent Research 9 (RR-9) science investigation was conducted by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Space Life and Physical Sciences program. The mission consisted of three experiments led by principal investigators Michael Delp, Xiao Wen Mao, and Jeffrey Willey. Delp’s investigation studied the effects of long-duration spaceflight on fluid shifts and increased fluid pressures in the head, Mao’s examined the impact of spaceflight on the vessels that supplied blood to the eyes, and Willey’s investigated the extent of knee and hip joint degradation caused by prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Specific aims of each experiment are summarized below.

The mission objectives

Michael Delp’s experiment had four aims:

To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS altered rodent basilar artery spontaneous tone, myogenic and KCl (Potassium Chloride)-evoked vasoconstriction, mechanical stiffness, and gross structure.

To estimate whether spaceflight on the ISS altered the blood-brain barrier in rodents, as indicated by ultrastructural examination of the junctional complex of the cerebral capillary endothelium.

To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS altered rodent basal vein (inside cranium) and jugular vein (outside cranium) spontaneous tone, myogenic and KCl-evoked constriction, distension, and gross structure.

To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS altered the ability of the cervical lymphatics to modulate lymph flow, and thus, regulate cerebral fluid homeostasis.

Xiao Wen Mao’s investigation had two aims:

To define the relationships between spaceflight condition-induced oxidative stress in reactive oxygen species (ROS) expression and retinal vascular remodeling and BRB function in mice that returned to Earth alive.

To determine whether spaceflight condition-induced oxidative damage in the retina was mediated through photoreceptor mitochondrial ROS production.

Jeffrey Willey’s investigation had two aims:

To determine the extent of knee and hip joint degradation in mice after 30 days of spaceflight on the ISS.

To use the DigiGait System to assess gait patterns before and after returning from the ISS.

IACUC Protocol Number: FLT-17-107

All animal procedures performed in these experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC), with protocol numbers NASA: FLT-17-107 for flight at the NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) and the Kennedy Space Center (KSC), and the methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.

NASA Space Biology Biospecimen Sharing Program Activities
N/A

Available Data

This portion of the Rodent Research 9 data collection contained environmental monitoring data for the Rodent Research experiment on the International Space Station (ISS), and in associated ground controls at Kennedy Space Center. It also included environmental and acceleration data pertaining to the SpaceX CRS-12 Dragon vehicle as it carried the Rodent Research payload to the International Space Station and back down to Earth.

The following environmental and acceleration data were included:

A reference document for the data collection

For ascent: Dragon body acceleration (m/s²) values

For ascent and descent: cabin pressure (psia), temperature readings from cabin air and duct sensors (degrees Celsius), relative humidity readings from cabin air and duct sensors (percent RH), partial pressure of carbon dioxide (psia), and partial pressure of oxygen (psia)

protocols.description: A cohort of 10 week-old male C57BL/6J mice (Jackson Laboratory) were launched in one Transporter (10 mice per side), transferred to Rodent Habitats onboard the International Space Station (ISS) and maintained in microgravity for ~33 days (the SpaceX Dragon docked period). No crew activities were required except for standard animal transfers between the Transporter and Habitats, and other activities required to ensure animal welfare, such as health checks and NuRFB replenishments. Prior to Dragon unberth, all mice were transferred into a clean Transporter followed by transfer to a Dragon capsule and then returned to Earth alive. The duration from splashdown to handover of the mice payload at the pier was approximately 24 hours. After handover of mice to the NASA Rodent Research team, the mice were immediately transported to the animal facility at Loma Linda University for conducting post-flight rodent gait assessment and dissections. The primary investigator teams, BSP teams, and Rodent Research dissection Lead and team conducted the dissection process at LLU immediately following a health check and specimen sampling and acquisition of walking kinematic data and intraocular pressure (IOP) measurements. A Basal Control (BSL) was housed in standard cages at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and euthanized one day after launch of the FLT animals. Ground Control (GC) and Vivarium Control (VIV) studies were planned to commence at KSC approximately one-week after the conclusion of the flight experiments. Early termination of RR-9 Ground Control (GC): Due to Hurricane Irma in September 2017 in Florida, the RR9 GC experiments were prematurely terminated. The study followed recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the protocol was approved by the NASA Flight Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
protocols.name: Animal Husbandry

protocols.description: Mice were euthanized, upon live animal return and dissected immediately. Each carcass dissection time was no longer than 1 hour from collection of the first tissue. Multiple tissues, including the thymus tissue, were collected from each carcass.
protocols.name: Sample Collection

protocols.description: RNA was extracted using the AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) following SOP 3.1-Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNa Mini with Qiagen RNase-Free DNase set. Homogenization buffer for RNA purification was made by adding 1:100 beta-mercaptoethanol to Buffer RLT (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) and kept on ice until use. Approximately 20 mg of tissue was thawed on ice, isolated using a scalpel, weighed and immediately placed in 700 uL of the Buffer RLT solution. Homogenization was performed using tissue homogenizing bead mix (Zirconium 2.0mm RINO Lysis, Next Advance) on Bullet Blender Gold 24 (Next Advance) for 5 minutes at 4C per SOP 2.1-Tissue homogenization Using Bullet Blender Gold Bead Beater. Homogenates were centrifuged for 3 minutes at RT and 14,000 g to remove cell debris. The supernatant from each sample was then used to isolate and purify DNA and RNA following the manufacturer protocol. RNA was eluted in 50 uL RNAse free H2O, and DNA was eluted in 50 uL EB buffer. Concentration for all RNA samples were measured using Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) with Qubit RNA BR kit following SOP 4.1-RNA/DNA/miRNA/cDNA Quantification using Qubit Fluorimeter. RNA quality was assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with the Agilent RNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following SOP 6.3-QC cDNA. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.
protocols.name: Nucleic Acid Extraction

protocols.description: ERCC ExFold RNA Spike-In Mixes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, Cat 4456739, v92), Mix 1 or Mix 2, were added on the day of library prep at the concentrations suggested by the manufacturer protocol. Protocol followed is SOP 5.2 Use of ERCC Spike-In Mixes and UMRR/UHRR Controls for Total RNA Sequencing. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.
protocols.name: Spike-in Protocol

protocols.description: All samples were normalized to an input of 10ng of total RNA and added to the QIAseq UPX 3' Transcriptome kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD), following SOP 5.4-QIAseq UPX 3' Transcriptome Library Preparation. Sample RINs greater than 3.0. Cell IDs, which are used to distinguish individual samples, are added to each sample during the RT step. This allows samples to be pooled together after the RT step and cary out library prepartion on a pool of samples as opposed to individual samples. An input of 50ng of pooled cDNA was used to carry out library construction. Library fragment size for this pool of samples is ~575 bp and was assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following protocol SOP 6.3-Quality Analysis of Sequencing Libraries Using 4200 TapeStation System with D1000 reagent kit. Final library concentration and pooled library concentration were measured by qPCR with the QuantSudio 6 Flex Real-Time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), following SOP 6.7-Sequencing Library Quantification using QIAseq Library Quant Assay. Library quality control was determined by iSeq100 (Illumina, San Diego, CA). GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.
protocols.name: Library Construction

protocols.description: RNA sequencing was performed by GeneLab Sample Processing Lab on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Asymetric paired end (Read 1: 93bp, Index: 6pb, Read 2: 28bp). PhiX included as control and to increase library diversity. Protocol followed is SOP 7.1-Setting up NovaSeq 6000 and iSeq 100 Sequencers. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.
protocols.name: Nucleic Acid Sequencing

protocols.description: Cell IDs, used to distinguish individual samples, were extracted from fastq files containing reads from multiple samples using UMI-tools (version 1.1.1). Extracted cell IDs were used to demultiplex fastq files to create one fastq file per individual sample. Raw fastq files from individual samples were assessed for % rRNA using HTStream SeqScreener (version 1.3.2) and raw fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1) and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports.
protocols.name: GeneLab raw data processing protocol

protocols.description: Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.0.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/tree/NF_RCP_2.0.0/RNAseq/Workflow_Documentation/NF_RCP). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) concatenated with ERCC92.fa from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip), and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf concatenated with the ERCC92.gtf file from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip). Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus + ERCC STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to forward and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0), ERCC genes were removed, and the non-ERCC genes were normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1). Assessment of ERCC spiked genes was performed as detailed in the ERCC_analysis_GLbulkRNAseq.html report.
